extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, public administrators, political scientists, civic educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and using governmental 'intelligence' bureaus, procedures for representative deliberation, and civic/administrative education so that public opinion and reason can function effectively in modern governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative index numbers for comparative measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn competition to ideal ends by inventing quantitative measures (index numbers) for the qualities you wish to promote so elements can be compared between workers, shops, factories, schools, departments, regiments, states, counties, and cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more you are able to analyze administration and work out elements that can be compared, the more useful competition becomes. 'Index numbers' are any device for the comparative measurement of social phenomena; good indices allow setting up competitions across many organizational levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central clearing house / diplomatic intelligence bureau
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a central agency (clearing house) to assemble facts suited to diplomatic or administrative problems and to obtain information from scattered departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than clerks or private secretaries piecing together scattered reports, the Department should call on its intelligence bureau which would and should obtain material from a central clearing house. This agency would become a focus of extraordinary information and expertise in terminology, statistical technique, and logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access of intelligence material to scholars and universities
rubrics_metrics.description: Make intelligence material (except a few diplomatic/military secrets) available to scholars so political science can use real-world research problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central agency could serve as the makings of a national university, recruiting staff from college graduates, running specialist appointments and exchanges with universities, and engaging students in research under consultation between curators and scattered teachers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and circulation to avoid institutional sclerosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure staff circulation between government departments, factories, offices, and universities to avoid dead weight, pedantry, red tape, and perpetual irritation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A system with circulation of men, data, and criticism reduces risk of 'dry rot'. Supplement permanent staff with temporary specialists and exchange lecturers; turnover helps avoid the attraction of 'soft jobs' and bureaucratic ossification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional coordination with comparable accounting systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate intelligence bureaus across federal/state/city/county and flexible regional combinations so that comparable accounting systems reduce duplication and reconcile autonomy with cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legal frontiers often don't coincide with effective environments (e.g., New York City metropolitan district), federations of bureaus and comparable systems allow municipalities to act together for shared functions like health and transportation without forcing central management over all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence bureaus should simplify governance by making social processes visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence work should reveal unseen processes, making the social process visible, assisting personnel to self-criticism and reducing personnel per unit of result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By making available the experience of each, intelligence bureaus reduce trial and error, limit the waste of special investigating committees, grand juries, reform organizations, and bewildered officeholders, and simplify previously 'invisible' complex systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design intelligence systems as tools for men of action, not to burden private citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of intelligence bureaus is to aid responsible administrators, representatives, and workers — not to force every private citizen to digest expert reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligence systems primarily assist those doing public business who 'can no longer do it by rule of thumb.' While they serve as general information and checks on the press secondarily, they should push the burden of expert interpretation away from ordinary citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus public scrutiny on procedure rather than technical substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Outsiders (private citizens) can best judge whether relevant facts were duly considered, whether interest groups were heard, and whether ballots/procedures were honest, rather than attempting to decide substantive technical relevance themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The outsider can ask whether the relevant facts were considered and whether groups were properly heard; for most cases he cannot decide what is relevant — thus the emphasis should be on ensuring correct and transparent procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize hearings/conferences with neutral chair and consulting experts
rubrics_metrics.description: When public disputes arise, organize conferences/hearings with a neutral chairman and consulting experts to confront partisans with facts and analyses rather than rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The neutral chairman should call for specific data (e.g., wage tables, budgets) to substitute for vague claims. If parties refuse to provide evidence, the chairman can state findings to the public and note refusals, enabling informed public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require production of documents and transparency; state public findings when refused
rubrics_metrics.description: Require parties to produce supporting books and accounts when claims affect public interests; if parties claim privacy/refuse, the chairman/committee should inform the public of findings and the refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if an industrial employer claims inability to produce books (private), the chairman can inform the public that certain worker groups fall below an official living wage and report that the employer declined to increase wages or to state reasons publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expert mediation to dis-inflate partisanship by converting slogans into measurable facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert mediation should disentangle partisan slogans (e.g., 'well paid', 'exploited') into concrete measures (wage tables, budgets) so non-entangled observers can judge the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chairman calls for official statistics and budget analyses to determine who can meet an average budget; parties' differing interpretations are then routed to standing committees or intelligence bureaus for technical appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ the Socratic dialectic under expert facilitators
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative bodies should use a mediator who forces discussion to engage with expert analyses, breaking through words to meanings in a disciplined dialectical method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Socratic dialogue must be conducted by men who have explored both environment and human mind — not merely rhetorical antagonists — to separate real perception from stereotype and elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangle emotive stereotypes by defining terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn sweeping emotive terms into specific named categories (e.g., specify which labor groups are underpaid rather than saying 'Labor is Exploited') so perceptions can be objectified and corrected by data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming makes ideas objectified and separable from personal identity; once defined and scrutinized, such ideas are more readily open to correction by new data and less bound to one's self-respect or broader allegiances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic/educational training in source criticism and introspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic education should teach pupils to examine sources (where dispatches were filed, correspondent names, authorities cited), to recognize censorship/propaganda, and to practice introspection about imagery evoked by words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should use the case method, comparative history, and anthropology to make pupils aware of stereotypes and codes; study of error acts as prophylactic and stimulates appreciation for scientific method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic collection of social knowledge accompanying action
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather social data routinely as part of decision-making (not haphazardly) because modern decisions require such information; accumulated data will support political science generalizations and civic education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The collection will grow because decision-making demands it; this results in a body of data that scholars can generalize and teachers can use as working models to prepare pupils for unseen environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide working models of the social system for teaching and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop models of the social system that teachers and administrators can use to make pupils and officials aware of how minds work on unfamiliar facts and how to deal with the unseen environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With such models, teachers can use case methods to teach habits of examining sources and recognizing stereotypes; without them, full preparation for modern world problems is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of appeals to reason in crisis and the need for stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning in politics requires long-run stability and time for civic education; in emergencies, immediate non-rational means (speech, slogans, force, compromise) may be the only practical options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because rational political ideas are still broad and thin, and individuals' behavior unpredictable, appeals to reason are especially limited in sudden crises — one must distinguish false crises from real ones and accept practical measures under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the communication challenge of expert authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts (the 'true pilot') cannot simply rely on their knowledge; they must be able to persuade and be recognized by non-expert groups whose time and capacity to learn is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education to create expert-recognizing publics takes years; in immediate situations there is no time to convert each citizen into an expert judge — institutional procedures and trusted mediators are therefore essential.
